newsitem.title: USA: Albright may bring new direction to U.S. policy.
newsitem.headline: Albright may bring new direction to U.S. policy.

text.p: Without a doubt, Madeleine Albright's appointment as first woman secretary of state in more than 200 years of U.S. history will change the face and style of U.S. foreign policy. It may affect substance, too.

She recently told reporters that U.S. President Bill Clinton would be more of an activist on international affairs in a second term and there seems little doubt that his increased involvement -- and a more activist U.S. role in general -- is her own preference.
Her confirmation by the Senate for the number one job in the cabinet is expected.
Quite apart from gender, the contrast with the man she will succeed as chief American diplomat -- Warren Christopher -- could not be more dramatic.
Christopher, 71, an eminence grise of the Democratic Party, is by training and demeanor a corporate lawyer, a painstaking negotiator known for caution and perseverence.

Critics say he failed to effectively articulate post-Cold War U.S. foreign policy goals and lacked the assertiveness needed to lead the fight for American interests, including with Congress, which decimated the State Department budget.
Too nice, too polite, too colourless, many gripe.

Albright, 59, is in many ways the opposite. As ambassador to the United Nations since 1993, she has distinguished herself as a forceful, passionate and outspoken exponent of U.S. foreign policy -- and the exercise of American power.

"In terms of style, she is going to be more dominating and assertive than Christopher both vis-a-vis the State Department and with foreigners as well," Helmut Sonnenfeldt, a foreign policy expert with the Brookings Institution told Reuters.

Where Christopher would pull punches, Albright seldom did. "Clinton's blunt instrument," one headline called her. A prime example was last February when she blasted Cuban pilots who shot down planes flown by anti-Castro activists from Miami.
"Frankly, this is not cojones," she said, using the Spanish word for testicles. "This is cowardice."
The comment scandalised some diplomats but made her something of a folk-hero among Cuban-Americans, whose votes Clinton courted heavily in the 1996 election.
Christopher seldom reveals his feelings publicly. But an upbeat Albright taught one ambassador the "macarena" dance in the U.N. Security Council after Clinton's re-election victory.
Some say she has been most effective in the bulldog role. At the United Nations, she has gone toe-to-toe with allies, as well as countries Washington considers bullies and rogues.
Unlike the current secretary, who speaks only English, Albright converses in French, Czech, Russian and Polish.

The daughter of a Czech diplomat who railed against totalitarianism, Albright is also staunchly anti-communist. Her background as an immigrant fleeing eastern Europe in the Second World War will bring new resonance to support for NATO expansion.

Despite experience teaching international affairs at Georgetown University and her post at the United Nations dealing with myriad issues, many establishment "foreign policy experts" -- most of whom are white men -- doubt Albright has the depth and stature needed for the job. More soundbite than substance, these critics complain.

But even Christopher, who was said to have favoured former Sen. George Mitchell for secretary of state, and former Bosnia peace-maker Richard Holbrooke -- who also was a top contender for the job -- praised Albright's appointment.
"I think she's tremendously qualified," Holbrooke told Reuters. Christopher called her the "ideal choice to carry America's foreign policy into the 21st century."
There is little doubt she had influence as U.N. envoy, especially persuading Clinton to get involved in Bosnia.
"In those areas where she disagreed with Christopher, the disagreement was invariably that she wanted a tougher position than he did, like on Bosnia," one administration insider said.
She tended to take positions less sympathetic to Russia than Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott and the president and she will remain cautious about dealings with Moscow, he added.
She lacks Christopher's Mideast experience and has no real expertise in Asia or economics, two key areas. But she may be more open to rethinking the tough U.S. policy on Iran.
Albright was long considered a front-runner to be the next secretary of state but her chances seemed doomed when Mitchell emerged as the favourite after the November election.

The support of women's groups and possibly also First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton was seen as critical in improving her chances. Many experts described Albright as the "default" candidate, the one left after Mitchell, Holbrooke and other male candidates were ruled out.
Like other women pioneers in their field, she will have to prove she is more than that.
